_note: Curated company cards. Company names and tickers found in headlines become clickable. Descriptions are deliberately qualitative — fleet counts and rankings go stale fast, so this explains what a company does and what drives it rather than quoting figures that will be wrong in six months. `match` lists the names to detect in article text.

companies.name: Frontline
companies.what: One of the world's largest listed crude tanker owners, running VLCCs, Suezmaxes and LR2/Aframaxes.
companies.position: A scale player kept heavily on the spot market, so earnings swing hard with rates. Part of the wider Fredriksen group of shipping companies.
companies.earns_when: VLCC and Suezmax spot rates rise, long-haul crude voyages lengthen, and bunker prices fall.

companies.name: DHT Holdings
companies.what: A pure-play VLCC owner — nothing but the largest crude tankers.
companies.position: The cleanest listed bet on one vessel class. Balances spot exposure with some time charters, and has historically run conservative debt.
companies.earns_when: VLCC rates rise, especially on Arabian Gulf to Asia routes.

companies.name: Okeanis Eco Tankers
companies.what: A Greek-backed owner of VLCCs and Suezmaxes with an unusually young, fuel-efficient fleet.
companies.position: Competes on efficiency — modern scrubber-fitted ships burn less and can use cheaper fuel, so they out-earn older tonnage at the same headline rate.
companies.earns_when: Crude rates rise and the gap between high- and low-sulphur fuel is wide.

companies.name: International Seaways
companies.what: A large US-listed owner operating both crude tankers and refined product carriers.
companies.position: The diversified option: crude and clean exposure in one company, which smooths the ride when the two markets diverge.
companies.earns_when: Either crude or product tanker rates are strong.

companies.name: Teekay Tankers
companies.what: Owner and operator of mid-size crude tankers, mainly Suezmaxes and Aframaxes, plus some product carriers.
companies.position: Focused on the mid-size classes that serve shorter regional routes, so it benefits from trade rerouting more than from sheer long-haul volume.
companies.earns_when: Suezmax and Aframax rates rise and crude trade patterns fragment.

companies.name: Hafnia
companies.what: One of the largest owners of refined product tankers, spanning LR2 down to MR and smaller.
companies.position: A product-tanker pure play that also manages commercial pools for other owners, giving it unusual market visibility.
companies.earns_when: Refining margins are fat, refineries run hard, and fuel travels further from refinery to consumer.

companies.name: Scorpio Tankers
companies.what: A large product tanker owner with a fleet of LR2s and MRs.
companies.position: Known for aggressive capital allocation — heavy buybacks and debt reduction in strong markets.
companies.earns_when: Clean product rates rise, particularly on long-haul diesel and gasoline routes.

companies.name: Ardmore Shipping
companies.what: A mid-size owner focused on MR and Handy product tankers.
companies.position: Smaller and more focused than Hafnia or Scorpio, with high spot exposure, making it a geared play on clean rates.
companies.earns_when: MR rates rise and regional fuel arbitrages open.

companies.name: Nordic American Tankers
companies.what: A Suezmax-only owner with a long history of paying dividends.
companies.position: A simple, single-class structure marketed to income investors, though the dividend tracks a volatile spot market.
companies.earns_when: Suezmax spot rates rise.

companies.name: Stainless Tankers
companies.what: Owner of small stainless-steel tankers for chemical and specialised liquid cargoes.
companies.position: A niche at the quality end — stainless tanks carry aggressive cargoes that coated tankers cannot.
companies.earns_when: Chemical production and trade grow.

companies.name: Capital Tankers
companies.what: A Greek-sponsored tanker owner listed in Oslo.
companies.position: Part of the recent wave of Greek owners using Oslo's deep shipping investor base to list.
companies.earns_when: Tanker spot rates rise.

companies.name: ADS Maritime Holding
companies.what: A small crude tanker owner.
companies.position: Tiny relative to Frontline or DHT, so a single vessel's fixture materially moves results.
companies.earns_when: Crude tanker spot rates rise.

companies.name: Performance Shipping
companies.what: A small owner of Aframax and LR2 tankers.
companies.position: A micro-cap where corporate actions and share issuance have mattered as much to shareholders as freight rates.
companies.earns_when: Aframax and LR2 rates rise.

companies.name: OMC Tankers
companies.what: A tanker owner listed on Oslo's junior market.
companies.position: One of several smaller owners using Oslo's Euronext Growth listing route.
companies.earns_when: Tanker rates rise.

companies.name: Volare Shipping
companies.what: A crude tanker owner whose ticker is, confusingly, VLCC.
companies.position: Worth knowing precisely because the ticker looks like a vessel class — in a headline, VLCC may mean this company or the ship type.
companies.earns_when: Crude tanker rates rise.

companies.name: Golden Ocean
companies.listed: Delisted from Oslo — merged into CMB.TECH
companies.what: Formerly one of the largest listed dry bulk owners, concentrated in Capesize and Panamax vessels.
companies.position: Historically the big listed Capesize play and part of the Fredriksen group. It merged into CMB.TECH, so Oslo no longer carries its announcements.
companies.earns_when: Capesize rates rise with Chinese steel demand (historically).
companies.note: Kept here for context because older headlines and course material still refer to it. Beware: on Yahoo Finance the ticker GOGL now resolves to a Google-linked ETF, not this company.

companies.name: Star Bulk Carriers
companies.what: One of the largest listed dry bulk owners, with vessels from Capesize down to Supramax.
companies.position: Diversified across the whole size range, so it captures both the iron ore trade and the steadier minor bulks.
companies.earns_when: The BDI rises broadly, not just in one class.

companies.name: Genco Shipping & Trading
companies.what: A US-listed dry bulk owner spanning Capesize to Handysize.
companies.position: Has pursued a low-leverage, dividend-paying model, unusual in a notoriously cyclical segment.
companies.earns_when: Dry bulk rates rise across the size range.

companies.name: 2020 Bulkers
companies.what: Owner of a small fleet of very large, modern Newcastlemax bulkers.
companies.position: A concentrated, high-specification bet — few ships, all large and fuel-efficient, with high spot exposure and a habit of paying out most cash.
companies.earns_when: Capesize rates rise and fuel efficiency commands a premium.

companies.name: Himalaya Shipping
companies.what: Owner of a fleet of modern dual-fuel Newcastlemax dry bulk carriers.
companies.position: A sister company to 2020 Bulkers in approach: a handful of large, efficient ships, LNG dual-fuel capable, run on index-linked charters.
companies.earns_when: Capesize rates rise and carbon rules reward efficient tonnage.

companies.name: Diana Shipping
companies.what: A Greek dry bulk owner with a fleet spread across the mid and large size classes.
companies.position: Traditionally favours longer time charters over spot, which dampens both the upside and the downside.
companies.earns_when: Dry bulk time charter rates are high when its contracts come up for renewal.

companies.name: Jinhui Shipping
companies.what: A Hong Kong-based owner of mid-size bulkers, listed in Oslo.
companies.position: A long-standing small-cap, concentrated in the Supramax segment.
companies.earns_when: Supramax rates rise.

companies.name: Klaveness Combination Carriers
companies.what: Operates combination carriers that can switch between dry bulk and liquid cargoes.
companies.position: Genuinely unusual and a great teaching case: by carrying wet cargo one way and dry the other, it slashes empty ballast legs and out-earns single-purpose ships.
companies.earns_when: Either dry bulk or product tanker rates are strong — and especially when its specific route pairings line up.

companies.name: Flex LNG
companies.what: Owner of a fleet of modern, large LNG carriers.
companies.position: Chartered out on medium and long-term contracts, making it closer to an infrastructure income stream than a spot shipping play. Another Fredriksen-linked company.
companies.earns_when: LNG charter rates are high at contract renewal, and LNG trade volumes grow.

companies.name: Cool Company
companies.what: An owner and operator of modern LNG carriers.
companies.position: More spot and short-term exposure than Flex LNG, so it feels the LNG shipping cycle more directly.
companies.earns_when: LNG spot charter rates spike, usually with wide regional gas price gaps.

companies.name: Golar LNG
companies.what: Focused on floating liquefaction — vessels that turn gas into LNG at sea — rather than plain transport.
companies.position: Has shifted from shipping towards infrastructure, so its earnings depend on long project contracts more than on freight rates.
companies.earns_when: Floating liquefaction projects are contracted and gas demand supports new supply.

companies.name: Awilco LNG
companies.what: A small Norwegian LNG carrier owner.
companies.position: A micro-cap with very few vessels, so each charter fixture matters enormously.
companies.earns_when: LNG spot rates rise.

companies.name: BW LPG
companies.what: The largest listed owner of very large gas carriers, moving LPG worldwide.
companies.position: Dominant in VLGCs and has also moved into LPG trading and dual-fuel propulsion, burning its own cargo as fuel.
companies.earns_when: US LPG exports to Asia grow and the Panama Canal runs freely.

companies.name: Dorian LPG
companies.what: A US-listed owner of very large gas carriers.
companies.position: A focused VLGC play, more spot-exposed than BW LPG.
companies.earns_when: VLGC spot rates rise on US Gulf to Asia routes.

companies.name: Avance Gas
companies.what: An owner of very large gas carriers, historically Oslo-listed.
companies.position: Has repeatedly bought and sold vessels to time the cycle, a clear example of shipping as an asset play rather than an operating business.
companies.earns_when: VLGC rates rise, and when it sells ships near the top of the cycle.

companies.name: StealthGas
companies.what: Owner of small pressurised LPG carriers serving regional trades.
companies.position: The small end of the gas market, driven by regional distribution rather than the long-haul US–Asia arbitrage.
companies.earns_when: Regional LPG distribution demand grows.

companies.name: Odfjell
companies.what: A leading chemical tanker owner and tank terminal operator.
companies.position: Chemical shipping is more contract-driven and less volatile than crude or dry bulk, with high barriers to entry from cargo complexity.
companies.earns_when: Chemical production and trade grow and contract rates reset higher.

companies.name: Stolt-Nielsen
companies.what: A diversified group spanning chemical tankers, tank containers, terminals and even aquaculture.
companies.position: More an industrial logistics conglomerate than a pure shipowner, so freight rates explain only part of its results.
companies.earns_when: Chemical trade and tank container logistics demand grow.

companies.name: Wallenius Wilhelmsen
companies.what: A leading operator of roll-on/roll-off vessels carrying cars and high-and-heavy cargo.
companies.position: Car carrying runs on multi-year contracts with manufacturers, so earnings are far steadier than tanker or bulker income.
companies.earns_when: Vehicle exports grow and contract rates reset higher against a tight ro-ro fleet.

companies.name: Höegh Autoliners
companies.what: A Norwegian car carrier operator investing in large multi-fuel capable vessels.
companies.position: Like Wallenius, contract-led — and a useful example of how emission rules are pushing owners towards ammonia and LNG-ready newbuilds.
companies.earns_when: Vehicle trade volumes grow and contracts renew at higher rates.

companies.name: MPC Container Ships
companies.what: Owner of small and mid-size container ships chartered out to liner operators.
companies.position: A tonnage provider rather than a liner: it rents ships to the likes of Maersk instead of selling cargo slots, so charter rates are what matter.
companies.earns_when: Container charter rates are high when its ships come up for renewal.

companies.name: SFL Corporation
companies.what: Owns a mixed fleet of tankers, bulkers, container ships and offshore units, leased out on long charters.
companies.position: Effectively a shipping lessor — closer to a leasing company than a shipowner. Another Fredriksen-linked vehicle, built for dividend stability.
companies.earns_when: Charterers stay solvent and it redeploys ships at higher rates.

companies.name: ZIM Integrated Shipping
companies.what: An Israeli container liner carrying cargo for shippers on scheduled services.
companies.position: A liner, not a tonnage provider: it sells slots and charters in much of its fleet, which makes earnings extraordinarily volatile.
companies.earns_when: Container freight rates spike, as during Red Sea rerouting.

companies.name: Navios Maritime Partners
companies.what: A large diversified owner across dry bulk, tankers and container ships.
companies.position: Breadth across three segments at once, which makes it a reasonable proxy for shipping as a whole rather than any single market.
companies.earns_when: Any of dry bulk, tanker or container markets are strong.

companies.name: Kinetics LNG Holdings
companies.what: An LNG shipping company listed on Oslo.
companies.position: Part of the continuing flow of gas shipping companies choosing Oslo for its specialist investor base.
companies.earns_when: LNG charter rates and trade volumes rise.

companies.name: A.P. Moller-Maersk
companies.what: The Danish container shipping and logistics group, one of the two largest liner operators in the world.
companies.position: Has pushed beyond pure shipping into end-to-end logistics, so its results depend on container freight rates and on landside contract work. Its decisions on Red Sea routing move the whole container market.
companies.earns_when: Container freight rates are high and global goods trade is growing.

companies.name: MSC
companies.what: The world's largest container line by capacity, privately held and based in Geneva.
companies.position: Private ownership lets it expand aggressively without quarterly scrutiny. Because it is unlisted, you read about it through chartering and newbuilding activity rather than earnings reports.
companies.earns_when: Container rates rise and it fills its very large fleet.

companies.name: Hapag-Lloyd
companies.what: The German container line, among the largest globally.
companies.position: Operates within an alliance structure, so its network decisions are made jointly with partner lines.
companies.earns_when: Container freight rates rise.

companies.name: CMA CGM
companies.what: The French container line and logistics group, family-controlled.
companies.position: Has diversified into air freight, ports and media. Another unlisted giant whose chartering decisions drive the market for smaller container tonnage providers.
companies.earns_when: Container rates rise.

companies.name: COSCO Shipping
companies.what: The Chinese state-linked shipping group, spanning container lines, dry bulk, tankers and port terminals.
companies.position: State ownership means it can act on strategic as well as commercial grounds, and it is central to Chinese trade policy.
companies.earns_when: Chinese trade volumes grow.

companies.name: CMB.TECH
companies.what: A Belgian shipping group built on the former Euronav crude tanker fleet, now spanning tankers, bulkers and low-carbon fuel projects.
companies.position: Important to know because Golden Ocean merged into it — a lot of dry bulk capacity moved under this name. Pushing hydrogen and ammonia propulsion harder than most owners.
companies.earns_when: Crude tanker and dry bulk rates rise.

companies.name: TORM
companies.what: A Danish product tanker owner, one of the larger pure clean-tanker fleets.
companies.position: Runs an integrated model doing its own commercial and technical management, and reports results closely tied to clean tanker spot rates.
companies.earns_when: Refined product tanker rates rise and refining margins are strong.

companies.name: D/S Norden
companies.what: A Danish owner and operator active in both dry bulk and product tankers.
companies.position: Operates far more ships than it owns, chartering tonnage in and out — closer to a trading house than a traditional owner, which makes it a useful read on market direction.
companies.earns_when: It calls the direction of freight rates correctly, in either market.

companies.name: Equinor
companies.what: Norway's majority state-owned oil and gas company.
companies.position: Not a shipowner, but a major charterer of tankers and gas carriers and the biggest supplier of pipeline gas to Europe. What it does with production shows up in European gas prices.
companies.earns_when: Oil and gas prices rise.

companies.name: Vale
companies.what: The Brazilian mining group, one of the world's largest iron ore producers.
companies.position: Matters enormously to dry bulk because Brazil is far further from China than Australia is. When Vale ships more, the same tonnage of ore creates far more tonne-miles.
companies.earns_when: Iron ore demand and prices rise.

companies.name: BHP and Rio Tinto
companies.what: The two largest Australian iron ore exporters.
companies.position: The short-haul side of the iron ore trade. A shift in Chinese buying from Australia to Brazil lengthens voyages and lifts Capesize rates without any change in tonnage.
companies.earns_when: Iron ore demand is strong.

companies.name: Trafigura, Vitol and Glencore
companies.what: The largest independent commodity trading houses, moving oil, refined products, metals and coal.
companies.position: Among the biggest charterers of tankers and bulkers. They profit from price differences between places and times, which means they create the arbitrage voyages that freight demand is built on — and they charter ships for floating storage when the market is in contango.
companies.earns_when: Price gaps between regions widen.
